national.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after global outage
national.summary: The outage affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hourslong episode had impacted some of their operations.
national.body:
Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after a massive outage that lasted for hours.

"We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions," the company said in an update on X.

Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.

The outage affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hourslong episode had impacted some of their operations.

Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems started appearing around midday Thursday in the U.S.

The Redmond, Washington-based company apologized on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was "not related to cyber" or artificial intelligence agents.

It said the incident "was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced" following a recent network change.

The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.

national.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status as cases surge nationwide
national.summary: The United States has lost its official measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years. Here's what to know.
national.body: The United States has lost its measles elimination status, researchers with knowledge of the decision confirmed to CBS News partner KFF Health News on Saturday. The decision from the Pan American Health Organization came after the U.S. recorded over 5,400 measles cases so far this year — more than double last year's total. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization, covering North and South America. The agency is set to hold a news conference on Tuesday. A country is considered as having eliminated the measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization.The United States did not meet that standard for the first time since 2000. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about a third of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and continue to spread. After a 30-year record of 2,242 cases last year, the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths, with some states reporting additional fatalities. The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where state health officials have reported more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths associated with the disease this year. New York and Wisconsin have each reported one death. Measles cases have been confirmed so far this year in 45 states and Washington, D.C. What does it mean to lose measles elimination status? A country or region loses its measles elimination status once its population immunity lowers enough that the disease's spread can be sustained, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder explained. When a country has measles elimination status and a high rate of vaccination, a case of measles or small outbreak will soon fizzle out. But when there are this many gaps in the population's immunity, there can be "ongoing chains of transmission," Gounder said. "It means that we're at risk of being exposed to measles and getting measles if we're not vaccinated," Gounder said. "It means ERs and pediatricians need to consider measles in anyone with a fever and rash, whether they've traveled overseas or not. And we may now become an exporter of measles to other countries." national.title: Thousands of flights canceled as airlines work to recover from nationwide ground stop
national.summary: The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when another key Federal Aviation Administration computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
national.body:
Will Weissert, Associated Press Will Weissert, Associated Press

Hallie Golden, Associated Press Hallie Golden, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Airlines across the U.S. worked to recover from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years that canceled thousands of flights Saturday, stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers, spread ripple effects around the world, and forced pro and college sports teams to scramble for alternate transportation.

New technology being added to the nation's air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, Trump administration officials said.

Planes were taking flight and landing Saturday, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. But the effects could be felt for days. Officials say the system will likely return to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.

WATCH: FAA issues rare nationwide ground stop due to 'extraordinary circumstances'

The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when another key Federal Aviation Administration computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday's stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.

national.title: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
national.summary: Chile's far-right President José Antonio Kast is facing mounting public anger, as rising fuel prices trigger transport strikes and protests across the country.
national.body:
A masked demonstrator prepares to throw a Molotov cocktail as police use a water cannon to disperse students protesting education policies, rising living costs and reduced sentences for people convicted of sexual offenses against minors in Santiago, Chile, Nov. 5, 2026. Esteban Felix/AP hide caption

SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.

José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.

It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.

The Americas Chile turns right: Kast inaugurated as nation's most conservative leader since Pinochet But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.

"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.

"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.

Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.

national.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
national.summary: Trump will discuss the "reduction of nuclear weapons" during the unprecedented talks, a spokeswoman says.
national.body:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.

It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react.

No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

national.title: Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia's main airport due to altitude
national.summary: The foreign ministry in Abuja says 6 Nigerians with underlying health problems have died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.
national.body:
Nigeria's government has cautioned its citizens, in particular those with medical conditions, against travelling via Ethiopia's main airport due to its altitude.

The foreign ministry in Abuja said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems had died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.

The city sits at an altitude of 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level, making it one of the highest capitals in the world. Bole International Airport is a major hub for travel between Africa, the Middle East and Asia, serving millions of passengers a year.

Nigeria said those with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were at an increased risk.

The Nigerian foreign ministry did not disclose the identities of the travellers it said had died, nor the cause of death.

It urged anyone with a health condition exacerbated by high altitudes to "exercise caution" when planning a journey via Addis Ababa and "obtain appropriate medical guidance" before doing so.

The ministry stressed that it did not want to discourage Nigerians from travelling through the Ethiopian capital.

Visiting an area at a high altitude can be dangerous for people with heart and lung diseases, as the air is thinner and so less oxygen can get into the bloodstream, experts say.

national.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
national.summary: The Ukrainian president says US envoys touted the exchange as part of efforts to end the war with Russia.
national.body:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The Ukrainian president's comments come after US President Donald Trump's envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.

Russia controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

national.title: What we know about the US ground stop and what to do if your flight is affected
national.summary: US officials say the disruption was caused by old equipment overloading and not a cyber-attack.
national.body:
The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks.

The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe.

How many flights were affected? The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.

The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.

More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.

Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.

The Federal Aviation Administration opened skies again at until 20:15 EST.

national.title: Second catch attempt for SpaceX Starship rocket
national.summary: The attempt follows an unsuccessful effort to catch of the rocket’s booster which instead came down in the ocean.
national.body:
SpaceX will decide later whether to try to catch the top part of its huge Starship rocket as it returns to Earth.

The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.

But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch, and instead the booster diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.

The top part, known as the Ship, is due to return to Earth at about 15:15 local time (21:15 GMT) on Saturday.

This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs.

The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:47 local time on Friday.

The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned.

A "go" was initially given by mission control for a catch attempt at the launch tower, but the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding.

national.title: Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries
national.summary: This is the second time Alaskans voted down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which voters first approved in 2020. A repeal effort in 2024 also failed narrowly.
national.body:
A voter walks into a booth at the Valley Bible Chalet to cast his ballot on Election Day, Nov. 3, in Indian, Alaska. Lindsey Wasson/AP hide caption

A ballot measure that would have repealed Alaska's nonpartisan primary system and ranked choice voting has failed, according to an overnight race call by the Associated Press.

This is the second time Alaskans voted down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which voters first approved in 2020. A repeal effort in 2024 also failed narrowly .

This year, though, Alaska's system was under intense nationwide scrutiny, due to the inclusion of two candidates with the same name on the four-person U.S. Senate general election ballot. That race appears likely to move on to a ranked-choice tabulation.

"Alaskans of all political stripes have spoken: They want the freedom to vote for any candidate, regardless of party, in every taxpayer-funded election," Nick Troiano — the executive director of Unite America, a philanthropic venture fund that invests in nonpartisan electoral reform — said in a statement before the AP call. "At a time when most general elections across the country are essentially coronations, the Last Frontier is showing that a better way is possible. It is time to honor the voters' decision and move forward."

Just a few states have nonpartisan primary systems that allow voters of all political affiliations to vote on the same primary ballot. While California and Washington's systems allow the top two vote getters to advance to the general election, Alaska's system allows the top four candidates to move on. Then, if no candidate gets a majority of the general election vote, ranked choice voting is used to determine the winner.

Elections Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins race for Alaska governor, replaces a Republican Opponents of Alaska's elections say the current system is confusing and can be manipulated.

Those opponents seized on this year's closely watched Senate race, in which an independent candidate named Dan Sullivan was alleged to be a Democratic-backed spoiler recruited to siphon votes that were meant for the Republican incumbent, also named Dan Sullivan.

This is the second time Alaskans voted down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which voters first approved in 2020. A repeal effort in 2024 also failed narrowly .

This year, though, Alaska's system was under intense nationwide scrutiny, due to the inclusion of two candidates with the same name on the four-person U.S. Senate general election ballot. That race appears likely to move on to a ranked-choice tabulation.

"Alaskans of all political stripes have spoken: They want the freedom to vote for any candidate, regardless of party, in every taxpayer-funded election," Nick Troiano — the executive director of Unite America, a philanthropic venture fund that invests in nonpartisan electoral reform — said in a statement before the AP call. "At a time when most general elections across the country are essentially coronations, the Last Frontier is showing that a better way is possible. It is time to honor the voters' decision and move forward."

Just a few states have nonpartisan primary systems that allow voters of all political affiliations to vote on the same primary ballot. While California and Washington's systems allow the top two vote getters to advance to the general election, Alaska's system allows the top four candidates to move on. Then, if no candidate gets a majority of the general election vote, ranked choice voting is used to determine the winner.

Those opponents seized on this year's closely watched Senate race, in which an independent candidate named Dan Sullivan was alleged to be a Democratic-backed spoiler recruited to siphon votes that were meant for the Republican incumbent, also named Dan Sullivan.

national.title: Man in his 70s diagnosed with heart defect usually found in infancy
national.summary: Carlos Perez's doctors didn't know why his heart was having trouble. Then a scan showed something they had never seen before.
national.body: Mechanic Carlos Perez felt fine as he finished up work at his car repair shop in June 2025. He sat down with a glass of water, planning to relax for a few minutes before heading home. Then, out of nowhere, his heart started pounding and his chest ached. When he tried to stand, "the world narrowed," Perez said. "I said, 'Oh, no way,'" Perez, 72, said. "It was coming in waves." Perez called his daughter-in-law, a doctor, and she recommended he go to the emergency room. His wife brought him to the hospital. There, doctors determined that he was experiencing atrial fibrillation, or AFib, when the heart beats irregularly. The common condition can be dangerous: If left untreated, it can lead to stroke or heart failure.Perez's heart rhythm stabilized after about 90 minutes. But no one could figure out why the irregularity had happened. A battery of tests found no obvious cause. Then an advanced scan looked at both sides of his heart. "One doctor came in, then two doctors, and then a whole bunch of doctors went into the room," Perez said. "I'm getting really concerned. And they said, 'No, no, don't worry. It's just that we've all read about it, but we've never seen a patient with this.'" An incredibly rare heart defect Perez had a rare congenital heart condition called cor triatriatum, where a membrane grows in one of the heart's upper atria and splits it in two, leaving the heart with five chambers instead of the typical four. Without treatment, cor triatriatum can cause pulmonary hypertension, or high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. That can eventually cause irregular heart rhythms, which can become life-threatening. The condition is rare: About 0.8% of babies are born with a congenital heart disease, Dr. Wayne Franklin, a cardiologist and the senior vice president of the Heart and Lung Center at Children's National Hospital, said. Cor triatriatum accounts for 0.1% of those cases, or about 1 in 10,000. Perez's case was even rarer. Cor triatriatum is almost always diagnosed in utero or infancy, and treated early in a person's life. If it isn't, it's usually found when a person is in their 30s or 40s, Franklin said. But Perez had somehow gone decades without any significant issues. national.summary: President Trump is looking to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals in the first formal trilateral between the leaders of U.S., China and Russia.
national.body: President Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting among the three leaders at a summit in China next week, the White House said Friday.The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.Mr. Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, officials said."The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.One of the major conflicts dominating Mr. Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the U.S. officials said."I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that U.S. envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky."China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.Mr. Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the president's return to power last year.The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal."We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on his trip to China but will not be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) before heading to Shenzhen.

national.title: Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister
national.summary: Prime Minister Péter Magyar promised a sweeping anti-corruption drive after ousting Orbán in April.
national.body:
Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Viktor Orbán, authorities have said.

Miklós Seszták, who served as minister of national development for four of the ex-prime minister's 16-year rule, is accused of accepting bribes as part of a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing.

Hungary's new Prime Minister Péter Magyar unseated Orbán in a landslide election in April on the promise of launching a sweeping anti-corruption drive.

On Friday, following the two-day search for the cash - found in secluded locations across the country - Magyar described it as the end of the "mafia".

Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses, as part of the probe into Seszták, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) said in a statement.

The cash amounted to "5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100", it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m. It has been deposited into the Hungarian State Treasury, the body said.

The NVVH was established to investigate allegations of corruption during the Orbán rule, which Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory".

Magyar promised Hungarians "regime change" during the election earlier this year and has set about undoing many Orbán-era policies since entering office.

national.title: As Democrats win big, thirst traps of male candidates take social media by storm
national.summary: It's everywhere on social media: Democrats celebrating the attractive men voters elected in the midterms. But it's bigger than a meme and says a lot about politics of masculinity in the age of Trump.
national.body:
If you're on social media, there's a good chance you've seen the videos: people getting hot and bothered about the young men Democrats just elected.

"I'm looking at you, Rob Sand. I'm looking at you, Jon Ossoff. I'm looking at you, El-Sayed," said fitness coach Jesse Barton, reacting to the midterm results . "I am looking, I am not the only one, and I'm very happy about what I see."

There are debates over candidates' relative levels of hotness. There are a lot of AI-generated images. And there are many, many montages of the politicians set to sexy pop music.

One of the most viral pieces of content was a parody Tiger Beat magazine cover featuring Democratic men … which Manoushka Guerrier, an LA-based chef and content-creator, took one step further.

"I created the entire Tiger Beat style personality quiz , complete with the different boy band personas," she said. The quiz gives people matches including "the Babyface" (Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico) and "the Heartthrob" (Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel).

View this post on Instagram Guerrier pays a lot of attention to politics, and she emphasizes that these guys' looks are just a bonus.

"They're young and they're ballsy and they're smart, and they're not just smart; they're brilliant," she says.

The tidal wave of attention on these young men creates a striking contrast to the first Trump midterm, in 2018. national.title: Hegseth's failed impeachment was a warning to Democrats. Where will they go from here?
national.summary: Democrats have been given a huge opportunity with majorities in both the House and Senate — but the balance of priorities, timing, messaging and discipline are all going to be major tests.
national.body:
Democrats are not in the majority yet , but the first post-election test of their ability to get things done was a failure.

The House was unable to advance an impeachment effort of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Eleven Democrats were no-shows for the vote. Based on the math in this vote: If those 11 had been there and if no more Republicans showed up, the attempt would have gone forward.

Now, for those who want to see Hegseth impeached, it's fair to ask why only one Republican was in favor of it, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who led the effort , especially after an election that saw GOP wipeouts in no small measure because of the Iran war? The GOP still controls the floor, so a Democratic speaker would have been able to leave the vote open longer for the 11 to be able to cast their votes.

Congress House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth But it's also fair to ask if this would have happened under Nancy Pelosi's watch? (Ironically, she was one of the 11 who didn't vote for advancing Hegseth's impeachment because she had flown back to San Francisco for a veterans' event.) Or if this kind of effort is what people want in the first place.

First, on the Pelosi point: The former House speaker and retiring congresswoman was known for the discipline she kept in her caucus. She knew where the votes were, who was voting how and why – and, most importantly, did not move forward with efforts that didn't have the votes.

Hakeem Jeffries, the heir apparent Democratic leader , is going to have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. His leadership and agenda priorities are going to be scrutinized and compared to Pelosi – and this wasn't a great start to this new era.

Second, on whether impeachments are what people want to see: it depends on which people. Certainly, the Democratic base — and some beyond that — wants accountability for the Trump administration.

Voters more broadly also said corruption was a top issue in the campaign. But walking the line between reasonable accountability and oversight versus impeachments is a potential tight rope.

national.title: A new policy could help solve the U.S. organ shortage. Critics say it's unethical
national.summary: New guidelines are supposed to protect organ donors in a retrieval procedure that keeps blood flowing through livers, kidneys, lungs and hearts. But bioethicists have troubling questions.
national.body:
The U.S. organ transplant system has approved the first national policy for a controversial procedure used to remove organs from hospital patients. The guidelines are designed to protect potential donors. But critics say they do little to improve safety and fail to address deeply troubling ethical concerns.

Health A new proposal for organ donation sparks concern The procedure is called normothermic regional perfusion, known as NRP . It can be used after a family has decided to withdraw care because there's no hope of meaningful recovery for the person. To perform NRP, doctors attach an external pump to a donor minutes after their circulation has ended and they've been declared dead. The pump restores blood flow to their hearts, lungs, kidneys, liver and other organs to keep them from deteriorating.

"The hope with NRP is that it increases the supply of organs and it increases the quality of the organs," says Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration , the federal agency that oversees the organ transplant system.

NRP could help solve the chronic organ shortage, Lynch says. More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to HRSA. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.

Critics, however, say NRP is unethical because it violates the Dead Donor Rule , which is the most important rule protecting potential donors. The rule says transplant surgeons can only take organs from patients after they are dead because of brain death or circulatory death. But because NRP restarts circulation, critics say the procedure reverses the very condition upon which the person has just been declared dead.

"In order to be dead by circulatory criteria it means we're not going to attempt to reestablish circulation. But that's exactly what they do in NRP," says Dr. Lainie Friedman Ross , a University of Rochester bioethicist. "So, yes, I have a real problem with NRP. I think it violates the dead donor rule. It's taking organs from people who are no longer dead."

Only on NPR Are you an organ donor? Here are some rule changes you may want to know The other aspect of NRP that troubles critics is what surgeons do to try to make sure the donor is also brain dead, after circulation has been restarted by a mechanical pump. They clamp off blood vessels that supply the head. But alarm bells started going off for organ retrieval teams when blood appeared to get restored – or "reperfused" – to the brain during some NRP cases.

national.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
national.summary: Efforts to address the underlying problem with Outlook, Teams and Copilot are complete, the tech firm says.
national.body:
Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption.

The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected.

The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.

Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent.

Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.

Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.

Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge.

national.title: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins race for Alaska governor, replaces a Republican
national.summary: Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state legislator, ran a campaign emphasizing bipartisanship in the the state that usually votes Republican. At 37, he'll be the youngest governor in the state's history.
national.body:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, has won the race for governor of Alaska and will replace the outgoing Republican. Here he's seen at a polling station at the University of Alaska Anchorage on Election Day. Eric Stone/Alaska Public Media hide caption

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from the small island community of Sitka, won the race for Alaska governor, according to a race call by the Associated Press. At 37, he'll be the youngest governor in state history .

Kreiss-Tomkins will replace outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a term-limited Republican who has been governor since 2018. The state's last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who left office in 2002.

Kreiss-Tomkins, known by his initials JKT, made his "high-energy, bipartisan, problem-solving approach" a centerpiece of his campaign.

He's said he plans to build an administration of Democrats, Republicans and independents and described himself at a debate as a "man of the middle." He was endorsed by three former governors — a Democrat, a Republican and an independent — along with Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski.

Alaskans have had enough of zero-sum partisan politics, he said in an interview just before voting at a precinct in Anchorage on Election Day.

"I strongly believe people just want things to work, and want people to work together," Kreiss-Tomkins said.

The AP race call came after over a week of counting votes , including those coming in by mail and from remote parts of the state. In the ranked-choice system the state uses, he faced three Republican candidates, including one backed by President Trump. Winning requires getting a majority of the votes.

The American Heritage had docked about two hours earlier for passengers to disembark. In a news briefing late Friday afternoon, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said 32 passengers from the cruise ship were taken to area hospitals for treatment, but none with critical injuries. No one aboard the tanker was hurt, Moreno said. New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said two of her officers were also hospitalized during the rescue operation, but were in good condition.There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, aboard the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port NOLA. Moreno said the tanker "lost control" and crashed into the cruise ship. Some people were seen in the water in life jackets or standing near the railing as the other side of the ship listed farther into the water. Videos that also began circulating on social media appeared to show a boy, about middle school age, biking all over town in a banana suit. So CBS News came to Linton to investigate and find out who and why, but it wasn't easy.Because Banana Man's other trademark is that he doesn't ever talk. "And I saw that it made a lot of people smile, and I like making people smile."Banana Man said that when he was younger, he dreamed of being a superhero. "But I didn't expect to be a banana," he said. But as a banana, he has so much more appeal. Linton residents have now thoroughly embraced the legend, and many even dressed up as him for Halloween. national.title: SpaceX's Starship soars into orbit after booster malfunction thwarts double catch attempt
national.summary: SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster malfunctioned and ended up in the water Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.
national.body:
SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster malfunctioned and ended up in the water Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.

Elon Musk's company had to lower its expectations when the first part of the double catch flopped.

Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster ended up in the Gulf of Mexico after an automatic abort. Despite the setback, the bullet-shaped spacecraft continued toward orbit. It will steer toward the pad Saturday for a similar grab, barring further trouble.

The Super Heavy v3 Booster 22 explodes upon being diverted to the water while retuning from the launch of a Starship 42 during the 15th test flight from the SpaceX launch complex in Starbase, Texas, Nov. 13, 2026. Photo by Joe Skipper/Reuters

It's the first time that the spacecraft will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower. If all goes well, the flight will last 22 hours.

The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.

Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship prepared to deliver 26 of the company's most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday's grand finale.

SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company's sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world's biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.

national.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
national.summary: Jojo was poached as an infant and grew up in captivity. His keepers want to find him a friend - but it's not straightforward.
national.body:
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.

More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.

Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.

Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.

Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".

local.body:
The North County Water District has its eyes on more of Fredonia's water customers.

Eric Wies of CPL, the district's engineers, first told their November board meeting that a recent switchover of customers east and south of the Routes 20 and 60 roundabout to NCWD water is "looking good so far."

He then discussed preliminaries regarding a switchover north of the roundabout.

Wies spoke of running a line north of the roundabout to eventually connect with the town of Dunkirk water infrastructure near the Thruway. The town of Dunkirk is a member of the NCWD, which is solely supplied by the city of Dunkirk.

CPL is conducting "early explorations" of getting customers north of the roundabout onto the line, Wies said. That area is currently served by Fredonia water -- though the village is planning a project to connect with the NCWD and shut its own water treatment plant and reservoir.

Wies noted that the conversation turned early to the difficulties around installing a water line under the roundabout, then down Route 60. He suggested an alternative: Bypassing the roundabout and running it through the Lake Erie Estates trailer park, located a few yards to the northeast.

Wies said another benefit of that alternative would be that NCWD could access grant money available for water improvement projects at housing developments. He said the trailer park's owners want to expand, but claim issues with their current water system prevent that.

Also, Wies said the new line would allow Brooks-TLC's new Fredonia hospital to access an alternate water source through the NCWD. Planners had promised an alternate water source for the hospital, currently under construction on East Main Street, in response to worries surrounding Fredonia's numerous boil order disruptions in recent years.

Maryann J. "Jackie" Olszewski, 87, of Silver Creek, NY passed away Wednesday evening November 4, 2026 at the Chautauqua Nursing and Rehab Center in Dunkirk, NY.

She was born in Buffalo, NY on June 19, 1939 the daughter of the late Stanley and Marie (nee Berger) Tytka. She married the love her life, John Olszewski on November 30, 1958 in Buffalo, NY.

Jackie is survived by her beloved husband for 67 years, John Olszewski; two loving children, Lynne (Steven) Schmitt of Fredonia, NY and Dr. John Olszewski III PHD of Cincinnati, OH; a cherished granddaughter, Katrina Hughes of Dunkirk, NY; a dear brother, James (Susan) Tytka of Silver Creek, NY; also survived by nieces & nephews.

She was preceded in death by a daughter, Rebecca Hughes and a brother, John Tytka.

Jackie graduated from Silver Creek High School in 1957. She worked for many years at M& T Bank in Silver Creek as a bookkeeper. She was co-owner with her husband John of Harrington Candies in Fredonia, NY.

In her younger years she was a very active member and past president of the Silver Creek Fire Department Ladies Auxiliary. She coordinated and volunteered at the Silver Creek Red Cross Blood Bank. Jackie was also a very active member of the Order of the Eastern Star of the State of New York. She held several different offices in Silver Chapter # 288 in Silver Creek. She was the Worthy Matron several different years. Served as District Deputy Grand Matron of Chautauqua County, Grand Color Bearer for the State and she was the Grand Representative of Alberta, Canada. She enjoyed traveling, visiting every district of the Order in New York State. Trips out west were frequent, with stops at National monuments, National Parks and casinos.

As per her wishes, there will be no viewing a Celebration of Life will be held at the convenience of the family. Interment will be private in Willowbrook Cemetery in Dunkirk, NY.

Arrangements have been entrusted to the Hole-Parker Funeral Chapel, 160 Central Ave. Silver Creek, NY. Please share online condolences at www.holeprkerfc.com.

local.body:
Within the next month, elected leaders in the city of Dunkirk are going to have a choice to make when deciding on Mayor Kate Wdowiasz's $32.2 million spending plan for 2027 that includes a 12% tax increase. It simply comes down to this: Does the council represent the citizens of the city -- its constituents -- or will it support the government on life support.

Our guess? Council will not think twice about passing on that hike to city residents.

We totally understand the reasons. No one wants to tell dedicated and long-term employees that enough is enough. Likewise, no elected official wants to have to lay off or cut positions.

Payroll costs in 2026 in the city budget were about $9.5 million for 152 workers. That figure, however, does not include the costs for benefits.

What we know is health costs are rising and salaries are increasing, which ups the expenses in those categories. All told, salaries and benefits total nearly $13 million.

Due to generous contracts, those costs are no longer controllable. They will just keep going up.

Residents in Dunkirk, living paycheck to paycheck or on fixed incomes, are the ones who will be affected the most once the budget is passed. It is the same path taken for 2025 -- one of least resistance.

Of course, councils have a history of making poor decisions. Who can forget the trio in 2021 who voted for $300,000 in bonuses from American Rescue Plan Act funds? They padded their pockets -- and staff members -- as though they deserved an extra reward for working through COVID.

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- The Buffalo Bills are off to their best start in 33 years, Josh Allen and the high-scoring offense are clicking, and they’re tied for the top record in the NFL.

In a season during which many things have gone right so far, the Bills know better than to overlook a struggling AFC East rival when they face the New York Jets on Sunday at MetLife Stadium.

“This is a division game on the road, it’s going to be as hard as it gets, right?” first-year coach Joe Brady said. “We showed that we can go on the road and win a hard game. We’ve got to go do it again.

“And if we think otherwise, then I’m not doing a good enough job.”

Coming off a 23-6 victory at Minnesota on Monday night, Buffalo is 7-1 -- tops in the AFC and tied for the NFL lead with San Francisco. It’s the first time since 1993 the Bills have opened a season 7-1 or better. A win over the Jets (2-7) -- who they’ve beaten in their past five meetings -- would give them their best start since 1991, when they began 10-1 on the way to a second straight Super Bowl appearance.

“We know we’re always going to get everybody’s best, as we should,” Brady said. “And we’re going to have to bring it to be able to come out with a win. We know it’s not going to be easy, but we wouldn’t want it any other way.”

The Bills lead the NFL in total yards and points per game, with their 256 points through eight games ranking as the third most by a team with a first-year head coach in the Super Bowl era, trailing only the Mike Martz-coached 2000 St. Louis Rams (330) and Sean McVay-coached 2017 Los Angeles Rams (263).

It would seem the ultimate mismatch for a team struggling as badly as the Jets, who have dropped four in a row, have a coach in Aaron Glenn sitting on a blazing hot seat and a slumping, underperforming defense.

It is with heavy heartsthat we share that Samuel L. Drayo, Jr. peacefully passed away on November 11, 2026 at age 85.

Sam was a proud life-long resident of the Village of Fredonia. He was born December 27, 1940 in Dunkirk, NY. He graduated from the Fredonia Normal School (campus school at Old Main-kindergarten thru 8th grade) and Fredonia High School in 1958. He graduated from Syracuse University in 1962, where he earned a bachelor's degree in political science. He completed courses at the Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs. He was a 1965 graduate of Syracuse University College of Law earning a Juris Doctor degree.

Sam served two years in the U.S. Army from 1966-1968, attaining the rank of Captain. He was awarded the U.S. Army Certificate of Achievement and National Defense Service Medal. He received an honorable discharge in 1968.

In 1968, Sam joined his Dad, Samuel L. Drayo Sr., and twin brother, David C. Drayo, in his family's Fredonia law practice. Sam's son, John D. Drayo joined him in 2008 and they practiced together for many years. Sam served as Village Attorney for the Village of Fredonia for 47 years from 1969 to 2016 and Village Attorney for the Village of Brocton from 2005 to 2015.

In 1984, Sam helped organize the Northern Chautauqua County Youth Hockey Association (Dunkirk-Fredonia Steelers) and was its first President serving in that role for 8 years.

Sam was kind and had a generous nature and always found time to help others with legal and personal matters alike. He loved to laugh and had a great sense of humor. In his later years, Sam enjoyed researching, writing, and speaking about Fredonia historical and civic topics, frequently publishing pieces in The Observer. He also enjoyed traveling and made many trips to Italy with his life partner, Margaret C. Roberts.

He was a member of the Dunkirk-Fredonia Rotary Club, the Knights of Columbus, American Legion Post 59 and St. Anthony's Roman Catholic Church in Fredonia, N.Y.

Sam is survived by his loving partner, Margaret C. Roberts of Hamburg, NY (formerly Margaret C. Partridge) and his two sons, Michael (Kristie) Drayo of Phoenixville, PA and John of Fredonia, NY. He is also survived by three beloved grandchildren, Joshua Grant, Henry Drayo and Sadie Kathleen Drayo and former spouse, Susan R. (Meister) Star. He was predeceased by his twin brother, David C. Drayo who passed in 1985 and his parents, Samuel L. Drayo Sr. and Sadie (Mooradian) Drayo.

First it was the girls team that found success, but this season the boys returned a group with plenty of potential and this morning at Queensbury High School they could see fulfillment in the New York State Public High School Athletic Association Class D cross country championships.

Clymer/Sherman/Panama is not only finishing strong, but the Wolfpack have been one of the top boys teams all season starting with a third-place finish at the Rocket Invitational in Titusville, Pennsylvania. local.title: No internet? No service? Western New Yorkers build off-grid messaging network
local.summary: A group of Western New Yorkers is building an alternative communications network designed to keep people connected during outages, severe weather and other emergencies without relying on either one.
local.body: What happens when the internet goes down, or service disappears?A group of Western New Yorkers is building an alternative communications network designed to keep people connected during outages, severe weather and other emergencies without relying on either one."We're just a group of nerds that want to bring a community together," said Ehren Reynolds, founder and director of Western New York Mesh Inc.The nonprofit is building a network using MeshCore and radio antennas, allowing users to send text messages over radio signals rather than through traditional internet or cellular networks."There are situations where disaster strikes or weather-related incidents come up, and it takes those services away," said Reynolds. "Having another form of communication that is available to me feels like something that should just exist."That's especially relevant in Western New York, where winter storms can knock out power and communications."We saw Verizon go down last year," said Andrew Gurr. "It took out phone lines for a lot of people for a long time. With our winter storms, being able to communicate with other family members and not rely on internet service or cell services is huge."Users can compose short text messages on a cellphone, laptop or another compatible device. They then connect to what Reynolds calls a "companion," which contains Bluetooth and LoRa radios.That connects a user to the repeater. There are now 90 repeaters across the region, 20 sponsored by WNY Mesh, including one installed on top of the Buffalo Museum of Science.The setup can be relatively simple — a battery, solar panel and radio antenna.A message can then travel from repeater to repeater across the network until it reaches its recipient.WATCH: No internet? No service? Western New Yorkers build off-grid messaging networkReynolds stressed that the network isn't intended to take the place of emergency communications."It's not a replacement for 911 by any means," Reynolds said. "But it's a way of communicating in the event that you don't have access to cell technology or internet technology."Western New York Mesh is a nonprofit and is looking to add members and raise donations as it continues expanding its network throughout the region.Here's a link to their website for more information.

local.title: 'Means more to the kids': County funds save Niagara Falls' after-school 4-H Club
local.summary: The 4-H Club at Abate Elementary School in Niagara Falls was in danger of shutting down. Now, county funding has come in to keep it going and even expand.
local.body: The 4-H Club at Abate Elementary School in Niagara Falls was in danger of shutting down. Now, county funding has come in to keep it going and even expand.Within just a few years, what started as a class project for Brittany Costa's third graders at Abate has blossomed into an after-school 4-H Club of 56 students. Over the last school year, the students did everything from hatching chickens to growing their own produce in gardens outside the school."It was a huge success last year. We did a lot of activities. We did a coat drive. We maintained the garden. We served the community with all the produce we grew by donating it to the city mission," club coordinator Brittany Costa said.Not only did their food feed neighbors in need, but also won awards at the county fair. The district sent about 20 kids on an August field trip to the fairgrounds."They had produce that they grew on display, and they won 10 blue ribbons of excellence for their produce," Costa said.However, the future of the club was in jeopardy after the federal grant funding that the club relied on expired after the school year."I was disappointed, but that's how grants go. They come. They go," Costa said. "[But] they said if you can find the funding, you can do it, and so that's what I did."Costa took that challenge and ran with it. Niagara County Legislator Sam Farruggia picked up Costa's call and found $1,700 in county money to keep the program running."There are community partnership funds that go to qualified organizations that are making a positive impact in our community, and this program is a picture-perfect example of that kind of thing," Costa said. "I remember when I was in third grade, being part of a gardening club. It really opened my eyes to the magic of watching something grow."The $1,700 will be given to the Grassroots Gardens WNY nonprofit organization to run the 4-H Club at the schools. The funds are enough to keep it running at Abate, but also expand to two other elementary schools: Bloneva Bond, which has a full greenhouse, and 79th Street, where Costa now works.WATCH: 'Means more to the kids': County funds save Niagara Falls' after-school 4-H ClubJoin the Niagara County Community News Facebook group to connect with neighbors and learn about what's happening in your community.

local.summary: Two dance captains touring with the Broadway production of "The Great Gatsby" — on stage now at Shea's through Sunday, November 15 — held a master class at UB's North Campus.
local.body: Two dance captains touring with the Broadway production of "The Great Gatsby" — on stage now at Shea's through Sunday, November 15 — held a master class at UB's North Campus. "We're so excited — I think we're learning New Money today, which is one of the fun opening numbers of the show," remarked Ryan Sokira, UB dance major."It's so inspiring," added Violet Schraver, UB dance major. entertainment.title: How the Biopic ‘Being Heumann’ Pulls Off Two Revolutions
entertainment.summary: With a punk-rock spirit and a trailblazing disabled cast, director Siân Heder and star Ruth Madeley bring a lesser-known civil rights uprising to life, while challenging the Hollywood status quo
entertainment.body:
Judy Heumann is just trying to cross the road in her wheelchair. It’s New York City in the 1970s, and the streets are chaotic. Traffic barrels past, pedestrians crowd the sidewalks, and the concrete curbs are steep cliffs. Unable to get her wheelchair up onto the sidewalk, she rolls in the middle of Madison Avenue, giving the middle finger to a city bus driver behind her who is laying on his horn.

Set to the propulsive guitar riff of Iggy Pop’s proto-punk anthem “The Passenger,” the opening sequence of Being Heumann — a new biopic about the disability -advocacy pioneer — introduces a woman who refuses to be dismissed and has zero patience for anyone standing in her way as she navigates through potholes, puddles, and pedestrians.

“You are not introduced quietly to this character,” says Ruth Madeley, who portrays Heumann. “You literally meet her in utter chaos and noise. She’s unfazed because she is doing that every damn day of her life.”

Denied access to school until she was nine years old because administrators considered her and her wheelchair a fire hazard, Heumann later sued the New York Board of Education for the right to become a teacher. Her fight for equal access grew into a lifelong crusade.

In 1970, she co-founded Disabled in Action , a grassroots advocacy organization, and went on to become a leading voice in the independent living movement. Her activism helped pave the way for landmark legislation including the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Audacious, confident, and fiercely determined, Heumann became known as the “mother of the disability rights movement,” helping to transform disability from a matter of charity into a question of civil rights .

Siân Heder, the 2022 Oscar-winning director of CODA , first encountered Judy Heumann in the 2020 Sundance-winning documentary Crip Camp . When she read Heumann’s memoir, from which the film takes its title, Heder saw a fascinating contradiction in a leader who demanded humanity from the world but sometimes struggled to recognize the limitations of those around her. In Being Heumann (now streaming on Apple TV), we see Judy charismatically inspire fellow disabled activists into action. And we also see when she pushes them to take on more risk than their bodies might be able to endure, like a hunger strike she urged others to take part in, even if that wasn’t wise considering their medical conditions.

entertainment.title: Daniel Kaluuya and Tyriq Withers go viral for bizarre airport interview amid nationwide flight chaos
entertainment.summary: The two actors were among the passengers stranded Friday night as planes were grounded across the US.
entertainment.body:
Daniel Kaluuya and Tyriq Withers are managing to give the internet something else to talk about following the FAA’s nationwide ground stop .

The two actors, who were among the passengers stranded Friday night as planes were grounded across the US, have since gone viral for a bizarre interview inside Eugene Airport in Oregon.

Speaking with KVAL News as the airport descended into chaos, Kaluuya, 37, and Withers, 28, recounted how they were forced to deboard their Los Angeles-bound flight.

“I just want to thank God and the FAA for protecting us, post-blue wave as well,” Withers said, seemingly referring to Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections , which saw the party take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

“It’s really upsetting me and my homegirl, ’cause if you can’t go to the airport, where the hell can you go?” he added.

Withers appeared to be referencing a viral 2016 news interview in which a partygoer famously said, “It’s upsetting me and my homegirl, ’cause we feel like, well, damn, if you can’t go to Bella Noche, where the hell can you go?”

The reporter interviewing Kaluuya and Withers couldn’t help but laugh before quickly turning the microphone toward Kaluuya, who said he felt “grateful.”

“Obviously, it’s an inconvenience, but I feel grateful … Think about how many lives were probably saved because of that decision,” he added.

entertainment.title: The 15 Best ‘Hunger Games’ Soundtrack Songs
entertainment.summary: Lorde, Patti Smith, Olivia Rodrigo, and Taylor Swift have all contributed music to the epic franchise
entertainment.body:
In the opening scene of The Hunger Games , before the battle and bloodshed, Katniss Everdeen comforts her sister Prim with a lullaby. “Deep in the meadow, under the willow,” she sings. “A bed of grass, a soft green pillow.” It only lasts a few seconds, enough to get out two simple lyrics, but it tells us what’s most important to Katniss, played by Jennifer Lawrence , and how she communicates. It tells us just how essential music is to the narrative about to unfold.

The Hunger Games franchise has grown considerably since the release of the first film in 2012. The four-part saga, adapted from the book trilogy written by Suzanne Collins, concluded in 2015. Since then, the franchise has expanded with two more book-to-film prequel pairings. The most musical of the batch, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes , received a theatrical release in 2023, while the latest installment, Sunrise on the Reaping, was released in theaters on Friday, Nov. 20.

Each film has arrived alongside eclectic, star-studded soundtracks that recruit artists with distinct interpretations of the highly emotional, hotly volatile story at the heart of The Hunger Games. They aren’t all soothing lullabies, mockingjay calls, or political anthems. But they are genre-spanning, and rich with characters we’ve seen go from the page to the screen. With original releases created by artists from Lorde, Patti Smith, and the Weekend to Olivia Rodrigo , Taylor Swift, and Bella Kay, here are the 15 best Hunger Games soundtrack songs.

“Yellow Flicker Beat,” the first song released from the Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 1 soundtrack, opens with an unsettling hum. In 2014, Lorde described the song as her first attempt at getting inside of Katniss’ head. From the beginning, the character served as a flicker of hope for the districts, but the worst nightmare who leaders in the Capitol never saw coming. All over the song, you can hear the threads of teenage angst and rebellion that colored Lorde’s debut album Pure Heroine . It’s present in the opening verse, when she compares her blood to rubies and precious stones, but especially when the chorus hits: “This is the start of how it all ends/They used to shout my name, now they whisper it.” — Larisha Paul

entertainment.title: 5 Apple TV Shows With All-Star Casts That Deserve A Bigger Audience
entertainment.summary: Apple TV has plenty of hits, but these five overlooked series pack serious star power and deserve a spot on your watchlist. Here's what to stream next.
entertainment.body:
In our endless quest to bring you the best that TV has to offer, today we're highlighting five Apple TV shows that deserve a bigger audience. These shows feature all-star casts, but if you missed them when they first came around, you're not alone. This list features a little something for everyone: Dark comedy, light comedy, mystery, and some good old-fashioned crime drama. Let us know in the comments below if you're already a fan of any of these series. Otherwise, it's time to update your watchlist.

Apple TV If you're a fan of "Orphan Black," it won't surprise you to hear that Tatiana Maslany delivers yet another amazing performance in the underrated Apple TV series "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed." Maslany plays Paula, a mom and recent divorcée who gets caught up in a dangerous criminal conspiracy. The bright spot in Paula's life is her sessions with cam boy Trevor (Brandon Flynn), and when she watches him get kidnapped during one of their sessions, she takes it upon herself to solve the mystery.

Maslany nails Paula's chaotic energy, and despite her poor decision-making skills, you can't help but root for her. Though Paula's antics are often over-the-top, Maslany roots her behavior in real human emotion, and it never feels out of character. The show also features Jake Johnson as Paula's ex and Murray Bartlett as a mysterious antagonist. With a second season on the way , now is the perfect time to catch up on "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed."

Apple TV Separately, Rose Byrne and Seth Rogen have both starred in great shows on Apple TV. Rogen co-created the brilliant Hollywood satire "The Studio," while Byrne was the face of the '80s-set dark comedy "Physical." Together, they star in "Platonic," which we ranked as one of the best comedy shows streaming on Apple TV . Byrne plays Sylvia, a stay-at-home mom who reconnects with her former friend, Will (Rogen), after hearing about his divorce. Unfortunately, this friendship makes Sylvia's husband, Charlie (Luke Macfarlane), jealous.

The series is committed to keeping Sylvia and Will's relationship platonic, exploring what a friendship between a man and woman approaching middle age can look like. The show makes use of Rogen and Byrne's contrasting energies, with Rogen typically seen as a chill, nice-guy stoner and Byrne tending to play more high-strung characters. Though it gets silly, "Platonic" is ultimately character-driven, and getting to know these folks is what makes the series so enjoyable to watch.

Nearly two decades later, Beyoncé shared rare details of her 2008 wedding to Jay-Z, revealing that their nuptials were a surprise for many of their guests.

Some of the A-listers that were reportedly invited to their ultra-private nuptials included Kelly Rowland, Gwyneth Paltrow, Chris Martin and singer Michelle Williams.

During the new interview, the star also shared details of her wedding dress, which was designed by her mom, Tina Knowles.

“My favorite dress my mother designed was my wedding dress—it was gorgeously simple and made with her love,” she said.

“Wearing a dress she designed was very important to me, and more important than any designer dress,” Beyoncé added.

entertainment.title: 10 Prime Video Shows Canceled Too Soon (But Are Still Worth Watching)
entertainment.summary: Like most streaming platforms, Prime Video pulled the plug on some fan-favorite shows too early, but you should still add these series to your watchlist.
entertainment.body:
Prime Video Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover With a plethora of series produced during the streaming era, so many shows on every platform are canned before they have a chance to build an audience. This trend extends to Prime Video which, for every hit show like "Reacher" or "The Boys," has multiple counterparts that got unceremoniously canceled. With this article, we're taking a look at the Prime Video original series that got their walking papers before they had the chance to deliver a satisfying ending. These shows might've built up their own loyal audiences, but that potential wasn't enough to save them from a premature end.

Whether it's quirky sitcoms or small-town sci-fi stories, Prime Video has pulled the plug on its fair share of underrated fan favorites. Even big-budget fantasy adaptations and spin-offs of more popular shows aren't safe from an earlier ending than planned. Each of these cancellations still hurt years later, with the shows deserving of getting a fuller run than they received. These are 10 Prime Video shows canceled way too soon but are still worth watching, even with their truncated length.

Prime Video Tig Notaro shines in whatever project she appears in, and she takes center stage for the short-lived original comedy "One Mississippi." In addition to co-creating the show with Diablo Cody, Notaro stars as Los Angeles radio host Tig Bavaro, who returns to her Mississippi hometown after her mother's death. Back in the bucolic community where she grew up, Tig reconnects with this rural world through the benefit of an adult's perspective. Despite positive reviews, the show was canceled after its second season, just as Tig and her love interest, Kate (Stephanie Allynne), become emotionally open with each other.

"One Mississippi" is one of the most underrated Prime Video original series ever , running for only 12 episodes. The laughs come in at a steady clip, but usually from an emotionally traumatized place, adding to their honesty and relatability. Notaro brings her penchant for comedic deadpan to her starring role, tempered with deep-seated vulnerability, particularly in Season 2. A relatively early casualty in Prime Video's original programming, "One Mississippi" feels like it was only it was still warming up.

Prime Video The superhero spoof "The Tick" has always been something of a cult classic, both as a comic book and a '90s animated series. After a live-action adaptation was attempted on Fox in 2001, the property received a live-action reboot in 2016 on Prime Video. In this version, the titular hero (played by Peter Serafinowicz) arrives in a nameless city to fight crime. The Tick is joined by his anxious sidekick, Arthur Everest (Griffin Newman), while meeting other heroes and villains with their quirky takes on the genre.
